A one-year GIC rate does not lock in five years: chart the renewal assumption

Compare five consecutive one-year deposits with one five-year deposit, trace annual interest differences and solve the later renewal rate that equates their final values.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare five one-year deposits with one five-year deposit

Interactive planning lab

Five one-year deposits: final principal plus interest$56,286.47
One five-year deposit: final principal plus interest$59,384.32
Constant later renewal rate that equates the endpoints3.38%

Original hypothetical five-year comparison, not quoted GIC rates. Both alternatives invest identical principal at time zero. One-year deposits pay all interest at each annual maturity; every dollar is immediately reinvested for another year. The entered first rate applies only in year one and the entered renewal rate applies in each of years two through five. The five-year deposit compounds at its selected annual rate and pays principal plus interest only at its final maturity. Intermediate locked-deposit values are accrued mathematical values, not accessible cash or redemption quotes. No tax, fee, default, deposit-insurance limit, extra contribution, withdrawal, early redemption, account rule or gap between maturities is modeled. The break-even later rate is a constant hypothetical rate for four renewals; it can be negative mathematically and is undefined when no principal is invested.

The central idea

A fixed rate applies to the term purchased. Reinvesting at maturity creates a new rate decision, so a higher first-year rate does not establish the better five-year outcome.

01

Separate the deposit term from the planning horizon

A household may have a five-year goal while comparing deposits with different terms. A one-year rate describes the first purchase. It does not by itself specify the return earned in years two through five, when another deposit would need to be purchased.

The OSC Investor Office’s GIC overview explains that a maturity creates choices, including reinvesting or taking the money in cash. This guide treats each reinvestment as a new purchase with an explicitly assumed rate. It does not assume the original rate will still be available.

The comparison starts each alternative with CAD 50,000 and ends both after five years. One buys successive one-year deposits and reinvests all proceeds at each maturity. The other buys one five-year deposit that compounds annually and pays everything at its final maturity. There are no extra contributions or spending withdrawals.

02

Read the rate calendar before the ending balances

Restore the example to give the first one-year deposit a hypothetical 4% rate and the five-year deposit a hypothetical 3.5% annual compound rate. The first-year interest amounts are therefore CAD 2,000 and CAD 1,750 respectively.

The one-year case finishes its first term at CAD 52,000 and appears ahead by CAD 250. The selected later renewal rate is 2%, however, and applies separately in each of the following four years. The five-year deposit keeps its original 3.5% compound rate under the assumed agreement.

The rate bars show that difference directly. This is an invented rate structure, not a statement about the current yield curve or the best available product. A real comparison needs dated quotes for the initial purchases and a clearly identified assumption for any future rates that cannot yet be locked in.

03

Reinvest the returned principal and interest exactly once

The rolling case’s five-year endpoint is CAD 50,000 × 1.04 × 1.024, or about CAD 56,286.47. Every annual maturity returns both principal and interest. All of that money buys the next one-year deposit, rather than being counted as an additional contribution from the household.

The five-year endpoint is CAD 50,000 × 1.0355, or about CAD 59,384.32. Under these inputs, rolling the shorter terms finishes about CAD 3,097.84 behind despite the higher first-year rate.

The value chart uses matching year-ends. The rolling balance is available at each annual maturity immediately before the assumed reinvestment. The intermediate five-year figures are accrued values under the compound formula. They are not promises of accessible cash or early-redemption proceeds. Comparing their heights alone does not establish that both choices provide the same liquidity.

04

Explain the final gap through annual interest differences

The waterfall compares interest earned in each year. It starts with the rolling case’s CAD 250 first-year advantage, then adds the later annual differences. The later figures use each alternative’s own accumulated opening balance, so they preserve the consequences of earlier compounding.

Adding those annual differences reconciles to the same negative CAD 3,097.84 endpoint. No separate deduction for original principal belongs in that bridge because both alternatives began with the same principal. Likewise, a maturity proceeds amount is not all interest: it includes capital already invested.

This decomposition helps locate the assumption driving the result. The first-year quote is not irrelevant, but it is only one part of a five-year sequence. If later renewal rates were higher instead, the outcome could change. The model isolates that possibility without claiming to know which future rate path will occur.

05

Find the constant later rate that makes the endpoints equal

The break-even calculation solves for one constant rate applied to each of the four renewals after year one. Its equation is (1 + first-year rate) × (1 + later rate)4 = (1 + five-year rate)5.

At the default inputs, the later rate is about 3.38% annually. A common later rate above that mathematical threshold makes rolling finish larger; one below it makes the five-year case finish larger, under the stated assumptions. The threshold is not a rate offer or a prediction of what an institution will pay.

The matrix replaces the first-year and later renewal rates while holding initial capital and the five-year rate selected. It retains signed final differences. A negative mathematical break-even rate can occur when the first-year advantage is already sufficient under the comparison; that does not imply a negative rate is available. With no principal invested, the two values are zero and the displayed break-even rate is unavailable.

06

Bring cash access and taxes back into the actual plan

A rate comparison should follow a cash-needs review. Annual maturities create decision points, but this tool assumes every dollar is reinvested immediately. Spending part of the proceeds would reduce later invested capital and require another schedule. An actual lock-in, redemption condition or renewal instruction also needs to be read from the agreement.

The calculations are before tax and fees. A taxable account can need tax cash before a compound deposit pays out; a registered account can have separate contribution or withdrawal rules. Those questions are outside this comparison. The illustration also assumes repayment as agreed and does not establish deposit-insurance coverage.

Use the four views to distinguish the term purchased, the rate assumed at each renewal, the accrued value and the cash actually released. The practical decision record should identify the initial quote, the future rate assumptions, the common comparison date and any earlier spending need. A higher rate on one short term is only one input to that record.
